Note Factory API Reference¶

Back to PlussQit API Reference

This reference teaches the free functions in pluss::note. They answer a different question from the Note method reference: how to build a text payload before there is a receiver to call a method on.

What pluss::note Is¶

Note is the text object in the PlussQit data-analysis stack. It carries UTF-8 text — or, in bytes mode, raw byte-oriented content — and supports shape-preserving, vectorized text manipulation and natural-language processing across scalars, columns, and small text tensors, the same way Series carries numeric values and Timeline carries instants.

pluss::note::* is the construction namespace for that object. Once a Note exists, every transformation is a method on it; these free functions only create one. The design mirrors pluss::series::* and pluss::timeline::*: the type and its factory surface are kept apart because “I need a Note” and “I have a Note, now what” are different jobs.

Choose By Intent¶

  • From text you already hold — make for UTF-8 text (scalar, a 1-D batch, or a small nested tensor); bytes when the content is raw bytes with no UTF-8 guarantee. pluss::make_note is the one flat shortcut kept for the common make-from-data case.

  • Shape first, one value — full (every cell a chosen string), empty (every cell the empty string), rep (the same, with the value written first at the call site).

  • Shape from an existing Note — full_like, empty_like, and the bytes-mode full_bytes_like, empty_bytes_like.

  • Generate content — rand (one random letter per cell), rand_between (random single characters in a range), arange (a stepped run of single characters), perm (character combinations or permutations of a word).

  • Split existing text — from_lines and from_words turn one string into a 1-D Note.

  • Assemble and choose — format fills a {placeholder} template; select builds a Note by ordered Series conditions.

  • Restore packed storage — unpack validates and reconstructs the stable binary envelope emitted by Note::pack().

  • Render — print produces a diagnostic representation (std::cout << n works too).

Reading The Signatures¶

Return type comes first, as everywhere in this reference. Where a parameter accepts several call-site spellings — a bare string literal, a braced list, a nested braced list, or a range — the pages document the canonical behavior first and then the overload quirks that change the result. make and bytes each collapse a wide set of historical spellings into one converted text parameter plus one explicit (flat, sizes) overload per source container.

Running The Examples¶

Every example is a runnable fragment (assume #include <pluss/pluss.h> and #include <iostream>), and every ### Output block is copied verbatim from the compiled program. To print a Note to the terminal, any of these three spellings works — they render byte-identical text, and the pages rotate through them so each is visible:

std::cout << pluss::note::print(n) << "\n";  // print(n) -> std::string
std::cout << n << "\n";                       // operator<< (default options)
pluss::note::print(std::cout, n) << "\n";     // print(os, n) -> the stream

pluss::note::print(n, opt) takes a NotePrintOptions for control over the layout — see print.

Examples that show a rejection call the factory inside a try block and print the first line of pluss::Error::what() (the message); what() also appends a Triggered at: location line, which the output blocks omit.

Reproducibility¶

rand and rand_between take a seed. A fixed nonzero seed makes the draw deterministic; the pages use seeded calls so their output is stable. perm, arange, and every other factory here are already deterministic.

Deterministic construction output is produced by examples/CodeN/note_factory_reference_demo.cpp; the binary round-trip and rejection cases for unpack are produced by examples/CodeN/tokenbatch_codec_reference_demo.cpp.

Every pluss::note::* factory has a page: the core constructors (make, bytes), the shape-first family (full, empty, rep, and the four *_like factories), the generative builders (arange, perm, rand, rand_between), the text-splitting factories (from_lines, from_words), assembly and rendering (format, select, print), and validated binary reconstruction (unpack).
